segments.text: It is a little past 2 in the morning at 266 Sandpiper Loop at Onipa Enclave, and The Nest is doing what every newsroom does at this hour, which is pretending to sleep.

The desks around me are dark, but none of them are empty, because there is a jacket on one chair, a cup of tea giving up the last of its steam on another, and somewhere behind me, a pair of headphones is still faintly humming.
You will meet some of the people who sit here, though not all of them tonight.
First, since this is a newspaper, you are owed the price. About 35 megabytes, which is cheaper than most arguments about football, and a good deal more useful.
This is the Gold Coast Palava.
In our part of the world, palava means trouble, an argument, a story too big for one mouth to carry, and Ghana has never been short of any of the three.

Each edition, we take one day, one event, or one decision from our past, and slow it down far enough to see what really happened, which usually means who was in the room, what the weather was doing, who was afraid, and who was lying.

Then, we look at what the rest of the world was doing at that very hour, because history looks different when you realize that two things you were taught in separate chapters were happening in the same week.
And finally, we bring it home to the Ghana you are living in right now, on your phone, in traffic, in the group chat, in the argument at the table on Sunday.
We cover four desks, so that politics, business, sports and entertainment, and life and culture each get their turn.
And each edition opens with a front page of quick, mixed headlines before we pick one lead story and go deep into it.
We speak mostly in English, with enough pidgin to keep us honest, and we promise to be serious about the facts and light about everything else.
Chale, make we show you what that looks like.

On the afternoon of January 22nd, 1824, in the forest near Bonsaso, on the south bank of the Bonsa River, a British governor named Sir Charles McCarthy stood with roughly 500 men facing an Asante army of about 10,000.

He was a soldier of French and Irish descent and a committed abolitionist, and he had walked his shrinking force through weeks of mud, with the rains having soaked much of his gunpowder and with the ammunition he had sent for still somewhere on the road.
The Asante army advanced in its famous fan formation and halted half a mile off, with the horns and drums of every chief filling the forest.
And then McCarthy did something that historians still struggle to explain.
He pushed his regimental band forward and ordered it to play God Save the King, apparently convinced that the anthem would shake the loyalty of the army in front of him.

Each time the music stopped, the Asante drums came back louder, so he had it played again, and then again, while his officers stood at attention and his soldiers watched, until the Asantes grew tired of the performance and answered with musket fire.
When the ammunition finally arrived and the boxes were opened, they were found to contain biscuits and macaroni.
That is what we call a lead story.
And this is what we call The Wire.

Seven weeks before the band played, on December 2nd, 1823, President James Monroe told the United States Congress that the Americas were closed to new European colonies, which became the Monroe Doctrine.
Six weeks after Bon Sasso, Britain would declare war on Burma and send an army into Rangoon.
And by May, Beethoven's Ninth Symphony would be premiering in Vienna with its ode to joy.

So in the very spring that Europe was learning to sing about universal brotherhood, an empire that thought it understood the world was losing a governor, in a forest it had never mapped, to a kingdom it had never taken seriously.

There is much more to that story, including what happened to the governor's head, what the Asantes made of the rockets that came two years later, and how it connects to a queen mother and a chair in 1900.
That will be a full edition, and I will not spoil it here.
So what is in it for you?
There are five things.
First, the details nobody gave you.

Most of us were taught history as a list of dates to memorize for an exam, and nobody mentioned that Ghana's story is full of weather, rumors, bad decisions, unlikely friendships, and very human fear.
Those details are what turn a date into something you remember at a dinner table.
Second, the world beside us.

Every edition sets Ghana next to what was happening elsewhere in the same week, so you can see where we were ahead, where we were behind, and where we were simply living through the same storm as everyone else.
Third, a way to read today's news.

When you have seen how a coup, a currency crisis, a stadium scandal, or a loud election actually unfolded the first time, you stop being surprised by the second time, and you start asking sharper questions of the people on the television.
Fourth, something to say.

Every episode ends with talking points you can carry into a group chat, a classroom, or a family argument, and we publish them on X and in short written editions on Substack so that what you learn does not stay in your head.
Fifth, a place to answer back.
This is not a lecture, and each edition closes with a question on our letters page.
The best letters from the comments section are read out in the next edition, so you are not only watching the paper, you are helping write it.
Now I should introduce one desk, because every paper is only as good as the people it makes uncomfortable.
Her name is Abba, and Abba talks.
She talks to me, to the printer, to the woman who sells plantain outside the gate, and to the generator when it dies in the middle of a deadline.
She also has a quiet plan she believes nobody has noticed, which is to leave Ghana, with the passport already renewed and the destination already chosen.
I gave her the 1824 file, expecting her to skim it.
She read it twice, and when she reached the part about the band, she stopped talking altogether, which, in the nest, is something close to a medical emergency.
She sat with her hand flat on the page for a long ten minutes, and when she finally moved, it was only to push the passport a few centimeters further from the edge of the desk.
I did not ask what it meant, because I suspect she is still working it out.
As for the other desks, you will have to wait, because a good newspaper keeps some of its sources to itself.
I will say only that one of them sits at a desk where the lamp is never switched on, because its owner has never needed it, and that another has not yet decided whether to trust me.
They will each be introduced when the story calls for them.
A country that does not know its own story tends to be told one by someone else, and this newspaper exists so that the next time someone tells yours, you will already have read it.
Here is our very first letter question.
What is one thing happening in Ghana today that you suspect has a much older story behind it?
Leave it in the comments, because it is pinned, and the best letters will help decide which lead story we open first.
Subscribe if you want the next edition to find you.
This is the introduction to the Gold Coast Palava.
Filed and signed at the Nest 266 Sandpiper Loop or Nipah Enclave and dispatched to Accra, to Kumasi, to Bungpurugu, to Hafasini, and to the world.
